b: Vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) — also known as Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV)
By far most common in AIDS patients ; its presence is used as a criterion for AIDS diagnosis
Virtually all KS lesions infected by HHV8 — a γ-herpesvirus like EBV
Transmitted sexually and via oral secretions/cutaneous exposures
HHV8 lytic infection: virally encoded G protein induces VEGF → endothelial growth; cytokines from inflammatory cells create proliferative milieu
Causative virus: Human herpesvirus 8 ( HHV8 , also called Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus/KSHV) — a γ-herpesvirus
AIDS-associated KS was the most common malignancy in HIV-positive individuals before the advent of antiretroviral therapy (ART).

snip.t: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, invasive cervical cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, and primary CNS lymphoma are strongly associated with HIV/AIDS.

| Kaposi's Sarcoma (pulmonary) | Cutaneous/mucosal KS lesions, pleural effusions, nodular/flame-shaped infiltrates on CXR, CD4 <100 | Presence of characteristic skin lesions, pleural effusions, specific radiological patterns, often less severe hypoxemia |
*Kaposi sarcoma:* Violaceous, non-blanching macules, plaques, or nodules on the skin, palate, or conjunctiva due to Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)-driven endothelial proliferation.

*Stage 4:* Severe symptoms (defining illnesses); HIV wasting syndrome, PCP, extrapulmonary TB, cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, Kaposi sarcoma, CMV retinitis, and chronic herpes simplex ulcerations.
Rashes, papules, nodules, ulcers: Direct manifestation of infection (e.g., Cryptococcal skin lesions, Kaposi's sarcoma in HIV, cutaneous leishmaniasis).

qs.q: A solid-organ transplant recipient on T-cell immunosuppression develops aggressive Kaposi sarcoma involving lymph nodes and viscera. What is the most appropriate initial management step to potentially induce regression?
o: Reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppressive therapy
Immediate radical surgical resection of all lesions
qs.e: Transplant-associated Kaposi sarcoma may regress with reduced immunosuppression. While other treatments exist, adjusting immunosuppression is a key specific intervention for this form.

qs.q: A patient with AIDS develops cutaneous violaceous nodules diagnosed as Kaposi sarcoma. How does the latent phase of the underlying viral infection contribute to this malignancy?
o: By inducing direct lytic destruction of endothelial cells to promote angiogenesis
By expressing viral proteins that drive cell cycle progression and inhibit apoptosis
By integrating into tumor suppressor loci to cause permanent gene silencing
By stimulating robust host production of anti-angiogenic cytokine inhibitors
qs.e: Latent human herpesvirus 8 infection produces viral cyclins and other factors that promote cell proliferation and block p53-mediated apoptosis. Direct cellular lysis is a feature of the lytic replication phase, not latency.

qs.q: Which form of Kaposi sarcoma is associated with a 1000-fold increased incidence compared to the general population and has seen an >80% decrease in incidence with antiretroviral therapy?
qs.e: AIDS-associated KS is the most common HIV-related malignancy, with a 1000-fold increased risk, and its incidence has dropped significantly with ART. Classic KS is not HIV-associated.

qs.q: An 82-year-old Mediterranean man presents with asymptomatic purple skin lesions on his lower extremities that have slowly progressed over several years. What is the most likely clinical variant of Kaposi sarcoma in this patient?
qs.e: Classic Kaposi sarcoma typically affects older men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Eastern European descent with an indolent course. The other variants occur in specific geographic regions or settings of profound immune deficiency.

qs.q: Which epidemiological form of Kaposi Sarcoma represents the most common malignancy in HIV-positive individuals prior to the widespread availability of antiretroviral therapy?
o: Classic Kaposi sarcoma in older men
qs.e: AIDS-associated epidemic KS, caused by HHV8, is the most common malignancy in HIV-positive individuals prior to ART. The other forms occur in different populations with distinct clinical presentations and epidemiological profiles.

qs.q: Which virus is specifically associated with the development of Kaposi's sarcoma in HIV-infected patients?
qs.e: HHV 8 is linked to Kaposi's sarcoma (KS), which is listed among the viral spectrum and malignancies. CMV and EBV cause other spectrums of disease.

qs.q: A 35-year-old patient with AIDS develops purple skin and mucosal lesions characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma. Which viral agent is strongly associated with this condition?
qs.e: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) is strongly associated with Kaposi sarcoma in AIDS patients, infecting B cells and endothelial cells. HPV types 16 and 18 are linked to cervical cancer instead.
qs.s: Essential Medical Virology: Structure, Classification & Replication: MCQs

qs.q: An immunosuppressed patient with HIV presents with Kaposi's sarcoma. Which viral pathogen is responsible for driving the proliferation of endothelial cells to cause this malignancy?
qs.e: HHV-8 drives the proliferation of endothelial cells, leading to Kaposi's sarcoma, especially in immunosuppressed patients. EBV is primarily associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

ai.summary: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumour driven by HHV‑8, most common in HIV‑positive patients. It presents as purple skin lesions that can spread to mucosa and organs. Early ART and local therapy control disease.

sections.p: Kaposi sarcoma is a low‑grade vascular tumour caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV‑8). Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by biopsy showing spindle‑cell proliferation and immunohistochemistry for HHV‑8 LANA‑1.
b: Purple or violaceous plaques, nodules, or ulcerated lesions on skin or mucosa

t.b: Shows spindle cells, vascular channels, and HHV‑8 LANA‑1 positivity – confirms KS
Identifies immunosuppression; HIV positivity is a key risk factor for KS
Low CD4 (<200) correlates with higher KS risk and severity

sections.p: The AIDS‑associated KS is staged by the AIDS‑KS staging system: T (tumor extent), S (systemic illness), and L (lymph node involvement).
b: T0: limited skin only; T1: visceral or extensive skin disease

t.b: Detects visceral involvement; absence of lesions suggests T0

sections.p: HHV‑8 infection is necessary; immunosuppression, especially HIV, allows viral reactivation and endothelial proliferation.

t.b: Positive indicates exposure; not diagnostic alone

sections.p: Patients develop violaceous patches or nodules on skin, often on lower limbs. Oral mucosa, genitalia, and visceral organs may be involved, causing pain or dysfunction.

faq.q: Is KS always linked to HIV?
faq.a: No, KS can occur in immunosuppressed transplant patients or rarely in immunocompetent people, but HIV is the most common trigger.
Complete cure is rare; control is achieved with ART and local or systemic therapy, but lesions may recur if immunosuppression persists.
ART reduces viral load and immune dysfunction, often shrinking lesions, but many patients need additional local or systemic therapy.
